'''''Cycas rumphii''''', commonly known as '''queen sago''' or the '''queen sago palm''', is a [[dioecious]] [[gymnosperm]], a [[species]] of [[cycad]] in the genus ''[[Cycas]]'' native to [[Indonesia]], [[New Guinea]] and [[Christmas Island]]. Although palm-like in appearance, it is not a [[Arecaceae|palm]].

==Etymology==
'Queen sago' alludes to the name 'king sago' given to the related ''[[Cycas revoluta]]'', as well as to its use as a source of edible [[starch]]. The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''rumphii'' honours the German-born Dutch naturalist [[Georg Eberhard Rumphius]] (1628–1702), who served first as a military officer with the [[Dutch East India Company]] in [[Ambon Island|Ambon]], then with the civil merchant service of the same company.<ref name=tcp>{{cite web |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/cycadpg?taxname=Cycas+rumphii |title=''Cycas rumphii'' |access-date=2010-12-05 |work=The Cycad Pages |first=Ken |last=Hill |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney |date=1998–2004 |archive-date=2007-11-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071112023841/http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/cycadpg?taxname=Cycas+rumphii }}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Rumphii1562.jpg|thumb|left|Bark]]

The cycad is a small tree, growing to about {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=on}} in height, with a trunk diameter of up to {{convert|40|cm|in|abbr=on}}. The bark is grey and distinctively fissured into rectangular, or diamond-shaped, segments. The [[leaf|leaves]] grow from the crown – bright green, glossy, palm-like fronds, {{convert|1.5|-|2.5|m|ft|abbr=on}} long, with 150–200 leaflets on each frond. The spiny [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] is {{convert|35|–|60|cm|abbr=on}} long. The male plant's [[strobilus]], or cone, is oblong-ellipsoidal, {{convert|30|-|60|cm|in|abbr=on}} long, orange in colour and foetid in [[odor|odour]]. The female's [[sporophyll|megasporophylls]] are about 30 cm long, fleshy, brown and densely hairy, with the fertile area about {{convert|35|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide. The seeds are 45 mm long and 30 mm wide, ripening from green to an orange- or reddish-brown colour.<ref name=tcp/><ref name=fao>{{cite web |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/abrs/online-resources/flora/stddisplay.xsql?pnid=7498 |title=''Cycas rumphii'' Miq. |access-date=2010-12-02 |work=Flora of Australia Online |first= |last= |publisher=[[Australian Biological Resources Study]] |year=1993 |archive-date=2012-10-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121025034401/http://www.anbg.gov.au/abrs/online-resources/flora/stddisplay.xsql?pnid=7498 }}</ref> In the [[Solomon Islands]], and perhaps elsewhere, the tree can "quite commonly" produce as many as a dozen major [[adventitious]] limbs.<ref>{{cite book | last= Dowe | first= John L. | date= 1989 | title= Palms of the Solomon Islands | location= Milton, Queensland | publisher= Palm and Cycad Society of Australia | page= 44}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The cycad's range is centred on the [[Maluku Islands]], extending northwards to [[Sulawesi]], eastwards to [[New Guinea]], and westwards to [[Java]] and southern [[Borneo]]. It also occurs on [[Christmas Island]], an [[Australia]]n territory in the [[Indian Ocean]] {{convert|300|km|mi|abbr=on}} south of Java, in Australia's Top End (Darwin), and in [[Western Australia]].<ref name="POWO_326820-2">{{cite web |title=''Cycas rumphii'' Miq. |work=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:326820-2 |access-date=2019-01-27 }}</ref> It is cultivated in [[Fiji]] and [[Vanuatu]]. It is largely a species of [[tropics|tropical]] closed [[forest]] or [[woodland]] on [[calcareous]] soils in coastal habitats.<ref name=tcp/> It is often found on stabilised [[dune]]s formed of [[coral]]line sand and [[limestone]].<ref name=IUCN/>

[[File:Cycas rumphii FemaleFertileLeaves BotGardBln0806b.JPG|thumb|left|Female plant with megasporophylls, or fertile leaves, at the Berlin Botanic Garden]]

==Relationships==
''C. rumphii'' is part of a [[species complex]] which also includes ''[[Cycas circinalis|C. circinalis]]'' from [[India]], [[Sri Lanka]], [[Indochina]] and southern [[China]], and ''[[Cycas thouarsii|C. thouarsii]]'' from the [[Seychelles]], [[Madagascar]] and [[east Africa|eastern Africa]]. Differences between these taxa, which have sometimes been considered conspecific, lie mainly in the shape and indentation of the [[Leaf#Large-scale features (leaf morphology)|lamina]] of the megasporophylls.<ref name=fao/>

==Uses==
The trunk of the cycad contains a starchy pith from which [[sago]] can be prepared by drying, grinding and washing. The seeds contain a toxic [[glucoside]], pakoein, but can be treated to become edible by pounding, repeated washing, and cooking. The bark, seeds and sap are used in [[poultice]]s to treat [[cutaneous conditions|sores]].<ref name=fao/> Called Namwele in the Kastom culture of Pentecost, Vanuatu, the plant is sacred, a symbol of peace and status.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Huffman |first=Kirk |date=July 1996 |title='Up and Over': The Opening of the Vanuatu Cultural Centre Complex's New National Museum Building |journal=Pacific Arts |volume=13/14 |page=52|jstor=23409779 }}</ref>

==Status and conservation==
Although the species is locally abundant, it is assessed as [[near threatened]] because it has undergone habitat loss across its range, and the population trend is decreasing.<ref name=IUCN/>
